Curfew is a small piece of software. It lets you set rules for how you use
your phone, and — this is the part that matters — it lets you set those rules
in advance, when you are calm, and apply them later, when you are not.

The design question behind Curfew is whether a person can make a binding
agreement with their own attention. Most attention-software answers no, then
sells the disagreement back as a feature. We wanted to know what the answer
looked like when it was yes.

## What we shipped

The first release does three things and refuses to do a fourth.

It lets you write a set of rules — no Twitter after nine, no shopping apps
on weekdays, no anything between midnight and morning — and lock those rules
behind a delay you choose at the moment of writing. Once the delay is set,
the rules cannot be revised faster than that. If you wrote a one-hour delay
and then change your mind, the change takes an hour to apply. The point is
not the delay. The point is that the version of you that planned ahead
gets to outvote the version of you that did not.

It records, with your permission, what you tried to open during a curfew.
Not as a guilt log. As a piece of information about which rules are doing
work and which are theater. The record is local. We do not see it. Nobody
sees it but you.

It refuses to gamify any of this. There are no streaks. There is no shaming.
There are no badges for compliance and no scoreboard for relapse. The
software's job is to be a calm instrument, not a calorie tracker for guilt.

## What the experiment taught

Two things that surprised us, written here so the next experiment can use
them.

The first: people did not ask for fewer rules. They asked for sharper ones.
A rule that said "no social apps after ten" was less useful than a rule that
named the specific app and the specific failure mode. Specificity is part of
consent. Vague rules turn out to be a way of not actually deciding.

The second: the delay was, for most users, the entire product. The locking
mechanism — the part we worried would feel paternalistic — was the part
people described as "the relief." A small finding, but a clear one. The
question of attention software is not how much it can do for you. It is how
much you can ask it to hold against you.

## What's next

A second release in the autumn that adds shared rules — a household-level
curfew that two phones agree to enforce together. The design question there
is consent at the boundary between two people who already trust each other,
which is a different shape of problem than the single-user case and one we
do not yet know how to answer well.

If you want to read more about how this connects to the studio's larger
question, the [mission](/colophon) is the right place to start.
